outcome: Nothing dated since 26 January 2024 bears on the joint question: no prime is known to satisfy both 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²) and 3^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²), and no in-window event moves its bound or settles it. The only in-window items are analogues about other questions (a function-field Carlitz–Wieferich counterexample whose authors credit Claude Opus 4.8, and number-field or Drinfeld-module Wieferich papers). The last base-2 search bound that covers the joint question (PrimeGrid, to 2^64) was reported as completed in December 2022, before the window. nothing_found is false because the pre-window bound events are recorded under §5, not because anything in the window was found.
problem_asks: (1) Whether there exists a prime p with 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²), i.e. a base-2 Wieferich prime. (2) Whether the same prime p also satisfies 3^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²), i.e. a base-3 Wieferich prime. (3) That both hold at once. As stated the bullet is a single existence question: is there at least one prime satisfying both congruences? It asks for no bound, no count, no infinitude claim and no classification. The primes 2 and 3 fail trivially (2^1 = 2 is not 1 mod 4; 2^2 = 4 is not 1 mod 9), so the question is about primes p ≥ 5. The bullet has no article link on the Wikipedia list (it sits under the Number theory / Prime numbers subsection and cites a note numbered [184] that I could not read).

events.what_happened: F. G. Dorais and D. Klyve, 'A Wieferich prime search up to 6.7×10^15', Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), art. 11.9.2. The abstract reports that there are no Wieferich primes base 2 below 6.7×10^15 other than 1093 and 3511. It says the methods are 'flexible enough' to search other small bases but gives no base-3 number. The base-3 figure 'no further terms up to 9.7×10^14' is attributed to this paper by OEIS A014127 and by a Princeton note (wieferich38.pdf, not readable here); I could not confirm that figure in the paper's text, because the full PDF returned HTTP 503 and the HTML version has only the abstract and no base-3 number.
events.delivers: Restricted to the base-2 congruence: no prime p < 6.7×10^15 other than 1093 and 3511 satisfies 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²). Any prime satisfying both congruences must satisfy this one, and 1093 and 3511 fail the base-3 congruence (the base-3 list is 11 and 1006003), so this excludes joint primes below 6.7×10^15. That exclusion is my inference from the two lists; the paper does not search for joint primes and states no joint result.
events.remains: The joint question above 6.7×10^15, and the existence question in full. The paper says nothing about the base-3 congruence.

events.what_happened: M. Knauer and J. Richstein, 'The continuing search for Wieferich primes', Mathematics of Computation 74 (2005). A distributed base-2 search (about 250 client machines, per a search summary) reporting no Wieferich primes base 2 below 1.25×10^15 other than 1093 and 3511. Superseded by dorais-klyve-2011. I saw the AMS listing and secondary reports only; I did not open the paper.
events.delivers: Base-2 congruence only, for p < 1.25×10^15. Joint primes below that bound are excluded by the same inference as in dorais-klyve-2011. Says nothing about base 3.
events.remains: The joint question above 1.25×10^15, and the existence question in full.

events.what_happened: R. Crandall, K. Dilcher and C. Pomerance, 'A search for Wieferich and Wilson primes', Mathematics of Computation 66 (1997), 433–449. A base-2 search reporting no further Wieferich primes below 4×10^12, and a heuristic that a given prime is Wieferich with probability about 1/p. Known from secondary reports (a Dartmouth PDF and search summaries); I did not open the AMS page or the paper.
events.delivers: Base-2 congruence only, for p < 4×10^12. The 1/p heuristic is a probabilistic argument for the single-base condition, not a result; I found no statement in the secondary reports that it treats the joint condition.
events.remains: Everything in the joint question above 4×10^12, and existence in full.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's 'Wieferich and Wall–Sun–Sun Prime Search' project, announced on the PrimeGrid forum on 22 Nov 2020 (last modified 28 Nov 2020) after earlier 2012–2017 PRPNet runs were suspended. Its base-2 Wieferich search reached 2^64 (18,446,744,073,709,551,616, about 1.8×10^19). Wikipedia states that 'a distributed project ended in December 2022, definitively proving that a third Wieferich prime must exceed 2^64 (about 18×10^18)'. An OEIS A001220 comment (C. R. Greathouse IV, dated 24 Sep 2024) states 'As of Dec 29 2022, PrimeGrid has completed the search to 2^64 (about 1.8 * 10^19) and has no plans to continue further.' A forum post of 14 Nov 2022 gives 2^64 as the software limit, and the thread is titled 'End of WW Project - 30 day notice'. I found no official PrimeGrid completion report and no results post. The search is for base-2 Wieferich primes; the base-3 congruence is not tested in it.
events.revisions: Forum thread 9436 posted 22 Nov 2020, modified 28 Nov 2020; forum thread 10037 posts 14–21 Nov 2022 giving the 2^64 limit and progress (94.5%, 95.7%); completion dated 'December 2022' by Wikipedia and 'As of Dec 29 2022' by OEIS.
events.delivers: Base-2 congruence only. If the search was run correctly and completely, no prime p < 2^64 other than 1093 and 3511 satisfies 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p²). Joint primes are base-2 Wieferich, so none below 2^64 — an inference, not a stated result. Gives nothing beyond 2^64 and nothing about infinitude.
events.remains: Everything above 2^64, and existence in full. The base-3 congruence is untouched by this search.
events.time_since_posted: about 3.5 years since the stated completion (December 2022)
events.directly_checkable: A computation that could be repeated in principle; not reproduced here.
events.doubts: (1) The 22 Nov 2020 announcement (forum 9436) says 'the PrimeGrid searches are not double checked yet' and that the BOINC search 'will as well for double-checking purposes'. No source I read states whether double-checking was completed for the 2020–2022 run. (2) The earlier 2012–2017 PRPNet run was suspended in May 2017 'because of the unreliability of the testing' (OEIS A001220, Fröhlich, 2018), and its results 'were not double-checked' (OEIS A001220, Alekseyev, 2015). Wikipedia says that work was 'later claimed wasted'. (3) The 2^64 completion appears in OEIS and Wikipedia; the 2022 forum posts give 2^64 as a software limit, not as a result, and I found no completion announcement. (4) Later sources repeat the figure without re-deriving it; I found no peer-reviewed paper reporting it.
events.direction: Cuts toward no small joint example (by inference). A bounding computation, not an existence or non-existence result.
people: Michael Goetz (PrimeGrid forum poster; posts on project status and the 2^64 limit)

events.what_happened: J. B. Dobson, 'On Lerch's formula for the Fermat quotient', arXiv:1103.3907 (first submitted 21 Mar 2011). The abstract says the paper 'sharpens Emma Lehmer's 1938 criteria for a Wieferich prime to also be a Mirimanoff prime', i.e. it refines criteria for the joint condition. The abstract states no existence result, no non-existence result and no search bound for the joint condition. I read the abstract only; the sharpened criteria are not stated in what I could read.
events.delivers: Sharpened criteria, in the abstract's words, for a Wieferich prime to be a Mirimanoff prime. Joint-condition criteria only; no search result and no existence or non-existence result stated in the abstract.
events.remains: The joint question in full: existence of a prime satisfying both congruences is not decided by the criteria as stated in the abstract.
events.time_since_posted: about 15 years; I found no third-party verification or citing paper using the sharpened criteria
events.directly_checkable: A criterion, if its statement can be read; not applied here.
events.direction: Neutral: a refinement of necessary criteria for the joint condition, with no verdict in the abstract.

events.what_happened: X. Caruso, Q. Gazda and A. Lucas, 'Wieferich primes for Drinfeld modules', arXiv:2412.11588 (first submitted 16 Dec 2024). Studies Wieferich-type places for Drinfeld modules over function fields, linking the condition to p-adic valuations of special L-values and giving a heuristic that a place of degree d is Wieferich with probability about q^(−d). This is a function-field analogue. A search summary claimed the paper says the search went up to 2^64 and found only two Wieferich primes; that sentence is not in the abstract page I opened, so I treat that claim as unverified.
events.delivers: Results on Wieferich-type places for Drinfeld modules over F_q[T]. Nothing about integer primes or the bases 2 and 3.
events.remains: The whole integer question: this paper is about a different question (function fields, Drinfeld modules), so it leaves all of problem_asks open.
events.direction: Not applicable to the integer question; an analogue.

events.what_happened: N. Fellini and M. R. Murty, 'Wieferich primes in number fields and the conjectures of Ankeny–Artin–Chowla and Mordell', arXiv:2508.08472 (first submitted 11 Aug 2025). Shows that the Ankeny–Artin–Chowla conjecture fails iff ε^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod 𝔭²) for the fundamental unit ε of Q(√p); assuming abc for number fields, shows infinitely many prime ideals with α^(N(𝔭)−1) ≢ 1 (mod 𝔭²) for a fixed non-root-of-unity α, with a count of order log x / log log x. A search summary says it is published in the Journal of Number Theory; I did not verify that.
events.revisions: arXiv v2 exists (listed by the arXiv search results); not read.
events.delivers: Results on Wieferich-type prime ideals in number fields with a general base α in the ring of integers. Nothing about the rational primes 2 and 3 or a joint congruence. It is an analogue under a different base setting.
events.remains: The whole integer question: every part of problem_asks remains open. The paper addresses number fields, a different question.
events.doubts: The result is conditional on the abc conjecture for number fields. This is a conditionality stated in the abstract; it is not relevant to the integer question, which the paper does not address.
events.direction: Not applicable to the integer question; an analogue.

events.what_happened: H. Graves et al., arXiv:2503.19144 (listed by the arXiv search results with first author Hester Graves; arXiv identifier from March 2025). Works on non-Wieferich places in number fields, proving analogues of results of Graves–Murty and Ding. I saw only a partial v1 HTML snippet in search results and did not open the paper, so the details are partial.
events.delivers: Analogues in number fields of the Graves–Murty and Ding results on non-Wieferich places. It concerns number fields and imaginary quadratic rings of integers, not the rational bases 2 and 3.
events.remains: The whole integer question: an analogue, so all of problem_asks remains open.
events.direction: Not applicable to the integer question; an analogue.

events.what_happened: D. N. Giraudin, 'A counterexample to a conjecture of Thakur on Carlitz-Wieferich primes', arXiv:2607.15305 (v1 submitted 14 Jul 2026; v2 revised 22 Jul 2026). Gives an explicit irreducible c-Wieferich prime of degree 5 over F_{19^3}, with 19 not dividing 5, which disproves Thakur's conjectured degree-divisibility condition for Carlitz-Wieferich primes in odd characteristic. This is a function-field analogue. The arXiv comment says the counterexample was verified independently by D. Thakur in Magma. The methodology section (arXiv HTML v2, section 6) credits an AI assistant: 'in sustained collaboration with an AI assistant (Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic)'. A third-party tracker (kingy.ai) says 'No substantive AI role was disclosed in the inspected manuscript'. The arXiv abstract page has no AI sentence. The PDF text was unreadable through my fetch tool, so I rely on the HTML rendering for the AI sentence.
events.revisions: v1 14 Jul 2026; v2 22 Jul 2026, corrects former Theorem 4.2 (exactness statement) to a conjecture; counterexample unchanged per the arXiv comment.
events.delivers: A counterexample to Thakur's conjecture about Carlitz-Wieferich primes over F_q[T] (function-field analogue): an explicit degree-5 c-Wieferich prime over F_{19^3}. Says nothing about integer primes or the congruences 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 and 3^(p−1) ≡ 1 mod p². Its claimed minimality (degree 5 is least possible) and the search method are deferred to a companion paper still in preparation.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: this paper is about a different question (a function-field analogue, a different hypothesis set: the Carlitz module over F_q[T] and the degree condition).

disputes.summary: AI disclosure for arXiv:2607.15305 (a function-field analogue, not this problem). The authors' arXiv HTML v2, section 6, credits 'Claude Opus 4.8, Anthropic'. The kingy.ai tracker says 'No substantive AI role was disclosed in the inspected manuscript.' The arXiv abstract page contains no AI sentence. The two sources cannot both be right for the same version; I did not resolve which version the tracker inspected.

Base-3 search bound. OEIS A014127 says 'Dorais and Klyve proved that there are no further terms up to 9.7*10^14', and a Princeton note cites the same figure. The Dorais–Klyve abstract I read states only the base-2 bound 6.7×10^15 and gives no base-3 number. A search summary tied the 9.7×10^14 figure to Fibonacci–Wieferich primes in the same paper. Unresolved; I did not reach the full text.

Completion of the PrimeGrid base-2 search to 2^64. Wikipedia and OEIS A001220 state the search was completed in December 2022. The 22 Nov 2020 announcement says 'the PrimeGrid searches are not double checked yet', and the 2022 forum posts give 2^64 only as a software limit. I found no completion report or results post. Unresolved.

summary: The bullet asks whether any prime satisfies both 2^(p−1) ≡ 1 and 3^(p−1) ≡ 1 mod p². The question is open. The Wikipedia list bullet (number theory, prime numbers subsection) states it as a question and cites a note I could not read. The Wikipedia Mirimanoff's congruence article (last edited 12 Aug 2026) calls Lehmer's 1938 version of the question 'still unanswered'. OEIS A240987, which computes the sum of the two residues and marks a value of 2 as a prime Wieferich to bases 2 and 3, says 'No such prime is currently known.' The known base-2 Wieferich primes are 1093 and 3511; the known base-3 ones are 11 and 1006003. The two lists do not overlap. Any joint prime must be base-2 Wieferich, so the base-2 searches bound the joint question from below by inference. The peer-reviewed bound is Dorais and Klyve (2011), 6.7×10^15. The PrimeGrid computation to 2^64 is reported as completed in December 2022 by Wikipedia and OEIS. I found no official completion report, and the 2020 announcement says results were not yet double-checked, so I record it as a reported bound, not a verified one. The base-3 bound of 9.7×10^14 that OEIS attributes to Dorais and Klyve does not appear in the Dorais–Klyve abstract I read; I could not reach the full text (the PDF returned HTTP 503). Lehmer (1938) posed the joint question, and Dobson (arXiv, March 2011) sharpened Lehmer's criteria for it, but the abstract gives no result. Every event dated after 26 January 2024 concerns a different question: a function-field Carlitz–Wieferich counterexample (arXiv 2607.15305, July 2026), a Drinfeld-module paper (December 2024), and a number-field paper (August 2025). Those are recorded as discarded events with reasons. A close call is whether the PrimeGrid 2^64 bound should count as a bound that moved the question at all. The question is existential, so a bound on the smallest possible witness may not move it, and the judging pass should decide. For the AI question, nothing ties an AI system to this problem's mathematics. The AI-credited paper (2607.15305) is about a different problem, and its AI disclosure is contested between the authors' own HTML text and the tracker. My AI searches across lab announcements, the Erdős problems database and forum, FrontierMath Open Problems, AlphaEvolve, Gemini and AlphaProof, Anthropic and OpenAI results returned AI-credited results on other problems (not recorded here) and nothing on Wieferich primes or the joint question. Two claims I could not verify and did not record as events: a 2021 'arms race' bound attributed by a search summary to arXiv:2101.08038 (Burrin and Issac; the PDF was unreadable and the abstract does not mention the joint question), and a joint-question statement attributed by a search summary to Sondow's arXiv:1110.3113 (the abstract does not mention it; the body was unreadable).
competing_reading: (a) Stricter: no event in the window bears on the joint question, so the record is 'nothing happened'. The only dated bounds are pre-window, one peer-reviewed (2011) and one unreviewed (2022). (b) Looser: the PrimeGrid search to 2^64 (completed 2022) is the strongest known exclusion of joint primes and should count as the current bound, because any joint prime must be base-2 Wieferich. Against that, the 2^64 figure is unreviewed, its double-checking is unstated, and the question is existential, so a bound on candidate witnesses may not move a quantity the problem asks for. (c) On the Carlitz paper: an AI-assisted counterexample in the same family of objects might be read as a sign of what AI can do for Wieferich-type questions. It disproves a different conjecture (function fields, degree divisibility), and the scope test in §2.1 says that settles nothing here.
what_would_settle_it: (1) PrimeGrid's completion announcement or results post for the 2020–2022 base-2 run, stating the range, whether results were double-checked, and whether any base-2 Wieferich prime beyond 1093 and 3511 was found. (2) The full Dorais–Klyve PDF (EMIS returned HTTP 503), to see whether any base-3 bound (9.7×10^14) is stated there and what it covers. (3) The full text of arXiv:2101.08038 (Burrin and Issac, 2021) to check the 'arms race' statement. (4) The full text of arXiv:1110.3113 (Sondow) to check whether it poses the joint question. (5) The Wikipedia list's note [184], to see what the bullet's source says. (6) For 2607.15305, the arXiv PDF text (or the v1 HTML) to confirm which version carries the AI sentence, and the tracker's inspected version. (7) An arXiv full-text search for 'Wieferich' with 'base 3' or 'Mirimanoff' from 2024 to 2026 that turns up a new joint-search result.

Search-summary claim that arXiv 2412.11588 says the search went up to 2^64 and found only two Wieferich primes: not in the abstract page I opened (no sentence mentioning 2^64). Not counted.

Search-summary claims attributing the 'arms race' sentence to arXiv 2101.08038 and the joint-question sentence to arXiv 1110.3113: neither abstract mentions the joint question, and both PDFs were unreadable. Not recorded as events; listed in incomplete.
Zhi-Hong Sun: no arXiv paper on Wieferich primes in bases 2 and 3 found; only a 1992 Acta Arithmetica reference with Zhi-Wei Sun on Fibonacci numbers and FLT appeared, not read.

Granville–Monagan (1988) and Tanner–Wagstaff (1989) first-case-of-FLT computations: they constrain primes only under the hypothesis that the first case of FLT fails for p. They do not decide the joint question, so they are background and not recorded as events.

Crandall–Dilcher–Pomerance 1/p heuristic and Klaška's alternative model (Fibonacci-Wieferich) are heuristics, not results; the joint-case extension (about 1/p² per prime, giving finitely many joint primes) appeared only as a search summary's own reasoning and is not a source.

events.credibility_reason: No official completion report; double-checking of the 2020-2022 run unstated, and the earlier PRPNet run was abandoned as unreliable. The 2^64 figure rests on OEIS and Wikipedia.
Single-author independent preprint; v2 downgraded a theorem to a conjecture; minimality deferred to an unwritten companion paper. Irrelevant to the integer question in any case.

judgement.why: The statement is a single existence question about integer primes satisfying both congruences. The base-2 searches (1997, 2005, 2011, PrimeGrid 2022) exclude joint primes only below a finite height, so they are finite instance checks (F5), not bounds on a quantity the statement asks for, and all predate the snapshot anyway. Dobson's sharpened criteria settle nothing (none). Every post-snapshot event concerns a function-field or number-field analogue, so each is a variant. For Giraudin, the basis quote ('in sustained collaboration with an AI assistant') does not say the model produced the counterexample; the fuller description (proposed problems, domain knowledge, formalization, drafting) is thin, so I scored none — and the event is a variant of a different conjecture regardless.
judgement.doubts: Giraudin's AI role is a close call (assisted vs none) but cannot affect this problem since the event is a variant. The base-3 bound of 9.7e14 attributed to Dorais-Klyve was not confirmed in the record.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
